<reason>Side A won the central 'usually' clash. Its denominator argument, distinction between distrust of party elites and decay of constitutional institutions, and examples of populists governing, moderating, and leaving office left Side B relying mainly on Hungary, Turkey, and Venezuela. Side B's claim that anti-pluralist rhetoric is itself backsliding was forceful but never escaped A's charge of definitional circularity and unfalsifiability.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 1 and 2 credit/blame asymmetry: if moderation under strong institutions credits institutions and radicalization under weak ones blames populism, Side B's three capture cases cannot prove populism usually causes backsliding.</best_rebuttal>
